pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 7-9 (Lower KS2/Grades 2-4): incredible insects — record-breakers and 'superpowers'. Dung beetles are the strongest animals relative to body weight; dragonflies among the fastest fliers; fleas jump 150+ times their body length; bombardier beetles spray boiling chemicals. The wow-factor of the insect world.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4 'Living things and their habitats' / working-scientifically (comparing, using data); primarily an engagement + comparison-of-measures topic.
• Standards — US (NGSS): supports 3-LS4-3 / structure-function reasoning and quantitative comparison practices.
• Operational details — the load-bearing cognitive move is RELATIVE-TO-SIZE comparison: a flea's jump isn't far in centimetres but is enormous per body-length; scaling to a human ('like leaping a skyscraper') makes it graspable. Tie feats to body structure (small size + exoskeleton + muscle leverage) so it's not just trivia. Great hook for the whole domain; keep the numbers concrete and comparative.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 7): names three insect record-breakers and their feats. Tier B (age 8): expresses a feat relative to human scale (flea-jump = person over a skyscraper). Tier C (age 9): explains WHY being tiny helps achieve extreme feats relative to size (less body weight to move; strength-to-weight).
bestPractices: Make feats RELATIVE to body size and scale them to the child's own body (flea-jump → clearing a skyscraper) so the numbers become graspable.
Tie each superpower to body structure (small size, exoskeleton, muscle leverage) so it's explanation, not just trivia.
Use concrete, comparative numbers rather than abstract records.
Leverage the wow-factor as a gateway/hook to the wider insect domain.
Distinguish absolute vs relative measures (a flea's jump is small in cm but huge per body length).
keyRepresentations: A 'Hall of Records' plate with tappable champions.
A scale slider mapping an insect feat onto a person.
A 'why can it do this?' structure-function callout.
commonMisconceptions: 'These feats are big in absolute terms' — they're extreme RELATIVE to tiny body size, not in metres/kilograms.
'Bigger animals are always stronger' — strength-to-weight favours the very small.
'It's just random trivia' — the feats follow from body structure and size.
'Insects are weak because they're small' — smallness is precisely what enables the records.
Confusing fastest/strongest/highest-jumping as if one insect holds every record.

learn.summary: For ages 7-9, this topic uses the wow-factor of record-breaking insects (dung beetle strength, flea jumps, dragonfly speed, bombardier beetle spray) to teach the core cognitive move: comparing feats RELATIVE to body size, not in absolute units. Learners name record-breakers, scale a feat to the human body (flea jump = clearing a skyscraper), and explain WHY being tiny and light enables huge feats per body-length. The discriminating understanding is separating 'strongest/fastest for its size' from 'strongest/fastest overall', and grasping that scaling an insect up would not preserve the feat because weight grows faster than strength.

activities.title: Insect Hall of Records: reveal the feat, then scale it to you
feedback: If a learner reports the raw number without a comparison, ask: 'How far would that be for YOU? Show it against something you know, like a building or a bus.'

If a learner treats a feat as a 'superpower' with no cause, prompt: 'A tiny body weighs almost nothing, and the flea's legs work like a spring-loaded catapult, so the push flings it a long way compared to its own length — being small and light, plus that springy launch, is the reason.'

If a learner says one insect holds every record, separate the categories: the flea is a jump champion for its size, the dung beetle a strength champion for its size, and the dragonfly one of the fastest fliers.
activities.rationale: Grounding records in human-scale comparison and structure-function reasoning is intended to turn memorised trivia into understanding of relative measurement, matching the topic's load-bearing move. A tappable/flap-reveal gallery is one concrete way to stage the reveal; the same learning can work with illustrated cards or a read-aloud comparison each child acts out against a known object. A sort of champion-to-record may check that classification but does not by itself elicit the scaling explanation.
sourceClaims: KS2 working-scientifically includes comparing and using measurements/data; this topic exercises relative comparison of measures.
learnerActions: Meet four record-breakers and their feats: one kind of dung beetle (the horned dung beetle, which can pull more than a thousand times its own body weight), the flea (jumps over 150 times its body length), the dragonfly (among the fastest-flying insects), and the bombardier beetle (sprays a hot, noxious chemical).

For each champion, first state the raw feat, then convert it to human scale: e.g. 'a flea's jump is like a person leaping over a skyscraper'; 'the dung beetle's pull is like a grown-up dragging about six double-decker buses (or you, a lighter child, dragging about two)'.
For each feat, answer a 'why can it do this?' prompt that links the feat to body structure: small size, light body, exoskeleton, and muscle/leverage.
Sort the champions by which record each holds (strongest for its size, a top jumper for its size, one of the fastest fliers) so no single insect is mistakenly credited with every record.
activities.intendedInsight: Numbers alone ('150 times', 'hundreds of times') mean little until mapped onto the child's own body; the human-scale comparison is what makes the feat astonishing, and the feat follows from body structure and size rather than being random trivia.

activities.title: Scale it yourself: slider and strength tester
feedback: If a learner concludes the flea moves a greater absolute distance than a person, clarify: in plain centimetres a person jumps much further; the flea only wins when measured against its own tiny length.
If a learner cannot explain the slider, ask them to read off both numbers: 'How many body-lengths?' versus 'How many metres?' and notice they tell different stories.
activities.rationale: A manipulable scale model lets learners vary the comparison and observe the ratio directly, supporting the distinction between absolute and relative measures. The slider and weight-stacker are optional concrete mechanisms; paper ratio drawings or acting out multiples of one's own height can achieve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: KS2 working-scientifically includes comparing and using measurements/data; this topic exercises relative comparison of measures.
learnerActions: Use a scale control that maps an insect feat onto a human in real time — slide a flea's jump multiplier and watch a person-figure leap higher and higher relative to known buildings.
Use a 'can it lift this?' strength tester: stack weights on a dung beetle and compare to stacking the equivalent ratio onto a human figure.
State in your own words what the slider shows: the feat is enormous measured in body-lengths or body-weights, even though in plain metres or kilograms a human moves or jumps far more in total.
activities.intendedInsight: Manipulating the comparison is intended to make the relative-to-size idea something felt, not just read: the ratio is huge while the absolute amount is modest, and these are two different claims.

activities.title: Would a giant flea still win? Reasoning about scaling
feedback: Correct answer to anchor to: the flea does not have stronger muscles than a whole person; a person's muscles are far more powerful in total. Being very small and light makes extreme feats possible relative to body size — a tiny body weighs very little, so its muscles and springy parts fling it a huge distance compared to its own length.
If a learner takes the record literally ('the flea is just stronger'), ask who could actually move a brick and name the two different claims: strongest FOR ITS SIZE versus strongest OVERALL.

If a learner thinks a person-sized flea would still jump 150 times its body length, discuss that weight grows much faster than strength when you scale up (qualitatively, not with precise multipliers), so the giant version could not do it.
activities.rationale: The second-tier 'why can something so tiny do this?' prompt discriminates genuine understanding of scaling from a repeated wow-fact, and the scaling counterexample surfaces the common misconception that abilities survive being enlarged.
learnerActions: Discuss the diagnostic question: a flea jumps about 150 times its body length, but a person cannot jump anywhere near 150 times their height — does that mean a flea has stronger muscles than a person? Explain what is really going on.
Argue whether a flea blown up to human size would still jump 150 times its body length, and why.
Give an example that separates 'strongest for its size' from 'strongest of all' — e.g. who could actually move a heavy brick, the person or the insect?
activities.intendedInsight: The record is a ratio, not a total; being small and light is the reason the feat is huge per body-length. Scaled up, the body would weigh far more (weight grows faster than strength), so the feat could not be repeated — the feat depends on being tiny.

activities.title: Brag battle: record-holders in role (optional extension)
feedback: If the brag drops the 'for my size' qualifier, prompt the learner to add it and say why the record would be wrong without it.
Steer boasts toward a stated reason (lightness, leverage) rather than pure spectacle.
activities.rationale: A short in-role dialogue can rehearse the key qualification and reasoning; it is a lighter engagement route and should supplement, not replace, the human-scale comparison work where the main insight lives.
learnerActions: In role, voice a record-holder insect boasting about its feat, then have it correctly qualify the boast: 'I'm the strongest — for my size.'
Challenge another champion so the group clarifies which record belongs to which insect.
Use the in-role talk to practise explaining WHY the feat works (small, light, exoskeleton leverage), not just that it exists.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the qualification 'for its size' into the insect's own boast is intended to reinforce the relative-versus-absolute distinction in a memorable, playful way.

constraints: Keep numbers concrete and comparative; the raw records are meaningless to this age group until scaled to the child's own body.
Always distinguish 'strongest/fastest for its size' (a ratio) from 'strongest/fastest overall' (a total) — this distinction is the main learning objective and the most common error.

Matching, sequencing and estimate-slider questions assess recall of facts and comparisons; they do not by themselves require a learner to construct the scaling explanation, so pair them with the discussion/explanation task.
The brag-battle dialogue is an optional engagement extension; it should not replace the human-scale reveal and the scaling-reasoning discussion.
Tie each feat to body structure (small size, light body, exoskeleton, leverage) so the topic is explanation, not trivia.
Slider, flap-reveal and weight-stacker are example mechanisms, not required tools; illustrated cards, paper ratio drawings, or acting out multiples of one's height serve the same ends.
Treat the square-cube scaling idea ('weight grows faster than strength') qualitatively for this age; do not assert precise multipliers.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; both listed sources are marked verified:false and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The records-facts source claim was removed from activity 1's sourceClaims because it establishes only topic facts, not the human-scale/relative-measurement teaching principle in that rationale; the facts themselves remain in the activity content.

The scaling claim 'weight grows faster than strength' (square-cube reasoning) is used qualitatively and is appropriate for this age; exact multipliers were not asserted and should not be presented as precise.

Specific records (dung beetle 'hundreds of times body weight', flea '150+ body lengths' versus the source's '100+', dragonfly speed, bombardier spray) come from general reference sources not independently re-checked here; treat figures as approximate.

The original row rated a 3D artefact 'poor' claiming '3D adds cost without conceptual gain' and framed the quiz as merely assessing; these are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened to scoped statements rather than propagated as universal claims.

probeDeeper: 'You said it jumps 150 body-lengths. Could a flea actually out-jump a person across a room? So what does the record really compare?'
'Why does being tiny and light HELP with a giant jump for your size?'
'If we made a dung beetle as big as a car, do you think it could still push 1000 times its weight? Why or why not?' (scaling counterexample)
'Is "strongest for its size" the same as "strongest of all"? Give me an example of the difference.'
assess.correctAnswer: No, it doesn't mean the flea has stronger muscles than a whole person — a person's muscles are far more powerful in total. What's really going on is that being very SMALL and light makes extreme feats possible RELATIVE to body size: a tiny body weighs very little, so its muscles (and springy body parts) can fling it a huge distance compared to its own length. Measured against its own size the flea wins, but that's because it's small and light, not because a flea is stronger than a human overall.

errorPatterns.pattern: Takes the record literally — concludes the insect is simply stronger/more powerful than a human ('a flea beats a person, so it's stronger')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two claims: 'strongest FOR ITS SIZE' vs 'strongest overall'. Ask who could actually move a brick — the person. The record is a ratio, not a total.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the flea has stronger muscles than a person
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the flea/dung beetle is stronger than a person full stop; misses 'for its size'

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the feats have nothing to do with size — the insect just 'has a superpower' with no reason
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make the scaling concrete: a tiny body weighs almost nothing, so a small push flings it far compared to its length. Being light is the reason, not a superpower.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: explains it as magic/superpower; can't connect small size to the big relative feat

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks if you made the insect person-sized it would keep the same super-abilities (a giant flea would jump 150 times a person's height)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Discuss: made huge, the body would weigh far more (weight grows much faster than strength), so it could NOT jump 150 body-lengths. The feat depends on being tiny.
errorPatterns.distractor: A flea as big as a person would still jump 150 times its height
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a flea blown up to human size would do the same jump; doesn't see that scaling up changes everything

responseLevels.gap: Concludes the insect is simply stronger/faster than a human, or treats the feat as a magic superpower with no reason.
responseLevels.full: Explains the record is relative to body size, that being small and light is WHY the feat is huge in body-lengths (not that the insect is stronger overall), AND transfers the reasoning — e.g. predicts a scaled-up insect could not repeat the feat because weight grows faster than strength.
responseLevels.partial: Says the feat is 'for its size' and names records correctly, but can't explain WHY smallness enables it — lists the facts without the scaling reason, or thinks a giant version would keep the ability.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A flea can jump about 150 times its own body length. A grown-up person can jump nowhere near 150 times their own height. Does that mean a flea has stronger muscles than a person? Explain what's really going on — why can such a tiny creature do such an enormous jump for its size?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who grasps the 'relative to size' idea explains that small + light is WHY the feat is huge in body-lengths, and separates 'strong for its size' from 'stronger than a person'. A child taking the record literally concludes the flea is simply stronger/more powerful than a human. The second-tier 'why can something so tiny do this?' exposes whether they understand the scaling (small body = little weight to move) or just repeated the wow-fact.
